Patricia — South Africa’s Oldest Working Steam Locomotive

By: Floris Kotze | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
A man, his train and their story!
This is not just another heritage item on display — Patricia is the oldest working steam locomotive on the African continent (built 1897, 128 years old). Its survival is thanks to one man, Clive Holliday, who personally invested a seven-figure sum and eight years of work to bring it back to life. The relaunch is both a celebration of South Africa’s rail history and a rare chance to see a Victorian-era locomotive run again — but its future is under threat because of high site fees and tension with Transnet.

Summary:
In 1897, Dübs & Company in Glasgow built a Class 6A engine for the Cape Government Railways. It was first numbered 194 under CGR, and in 1912 renumbered SAR 473 when the Union of South Africa was formed.

Today it is privately owned by Clive Holliday. He bought the locomotive in 2016 and began restoring it at Germiston Steam Depot. Every part has been repaired or replaced. After years of work, it is now back in working condition.

Our main character is Clive Holliday

Clive is a private collector and rail-heritage enthusiast. He believes in preserving South Africa’s steam history. He didn’t buy this train for money or fame. He bought it because it matters — for history, for the people who remember, for those who will see it move. He committed a seven-figure sum. He committed years of work. He pushed through when parts were hard to find. He dealt with logistics, old metal, old drawings, restoration teams.

Challenges
• Restoration was expensive and complex.
• He had to work with Transnet Engineering to use the Germiston Steam Depot.
• Now there is a dispute: he is being charged high monthly site fees. The space needed is large. Some of it is unused by him, yet he pays for all.
• If the fees stay high, or if he is forced off the site, the future of Patricia could be in danger.

Relaunch Event

Patricia will be relaunched on Saturday, 20 September 2025 at 10:00 AM at Old Germiston Steam Depot. It will be a public event to mark the completion of the full nut-and-bolt restoration.

This is a story about history, a man’s resolve, and a locomotive that has been given a second life.
But what now? It is finished and what happens next?

Script:


(Govan) When you think of South African railways, you think of a broken or dying industry. But I've come to this old train depot in Germiston to witness a resurrection.

(Clive) My name is Clive Holliday. I'm from the UK, obviously. I lived there for 60 years after leaving school. Then I started work on the railways.

(Govan) Obviously, you prefer South Africa over England, yeah?
(Clive) Certainly prefer South Africa over England, yes. And support the Springboks.

(Govan) In 2017, Clive found an old steam locomotive abandoned in Germiston, rusty and broken. Yet smitten, he decided to buy it. Only later did he discover it was over 120 years old and full of surprises.

(Clive) When I bought it, it was completely derelict. It was literally a boiler on wheels with no fittings, no copper pipe. It was just a very, very sad derelict engine. She was built in 1897.
I actually have some photographs when it was used during the Anglo-Boer War. One photo I have of it was standing at Mafiking at the head of an armoured troop train.

(Govan) These old photos, brought to life by AI, offer a glimpse of this world all those years ago.

From the railways of the early 1900s to today, 128 years later, another milestone has arrived for this once forgotten steam engine.

(Govan) The way that the steam was coming out now is really impressive.
(Clive) She’s raring to go, yes.
(Govan) This looks very cool. She's raring to go.
(Clive) Raring to go.

(Govan) Heritage Month marks her return - the result of seven years of restoration.
At the controls is Sean Ackerman, the man who, with his small team, turned Clive’s dream into reality.

(Govan) That's how you know people are impressed in 2025. They don't give a round of applause. They all take their phones out. To capture the moment. And this certainly is worth it.

(Shaun) A lot of people say steam locomotives are alive because of the natural resources that they use, water, coal, oil. The minute you put a locomotive to steam, you can actually feel, you know, it's a living machine. And when it moves, it definitely shows you that.

(Govan) Sean has come to know this steam train’s every nut and bolt. His small team has rebuilt her piece by piece.

(Shaun) In a lot of senses, it's newer than what it was when it was built, to be honest. But we've done a lot of changes to it. Not visual changes. You can't see it from a picture. But modifications using more modern materials, which just gives you a bit more, you know, running time. You don't need to do as much maintenance. We've done a whole lot of processes to improve it.

(Govan) It’s the newest oldest train in South Africa.
(Shaun) Pretty much yes, in Africa for that matter I think.
(Govan) In Africa?
(Shaun) Yes, yeah.

(Govan) How much did you pay to restore it?
(Clive) It was in excess of two million rand.
(Govan Two million rand for the love of it?
(Clive) For the love of it.
(Govan) Oh, that's an incredible investment there. There is some criticism people call these trains rich white people's toys.
(Clive) I have heard that comment on more than one occasion. Nothing could be further from the truth in my books. I mean, these locomotives were used to build South Africa into what it is now. And I firmly believe that that fact should be recognised and that we should preserve this for future generations to see and understand.
(Govan) Where would one likely see this train in the months to come?
( Clive) We're hoping to see this down in Mosselbay by the end of the year. Hopefully in time for the Christmas holiday period when there will be thousands of people from Gauteng who will be down in Mosselbay enjoying their Christmas break.

(Govan) I have done a couple of stories about trains and I got to tell you the people that have worked on steam trains take great pride in it and they say they place the the steam train above all other trains.

(Shaun) A lot of a lot of times you guys places in front of their wives I think - not in my case though!

(Clive) But it's quite an emotional day for me. The locomotive’s name, as you can see, is Patricia. Patricia was my mother. And it was because of her legacy that I was able to do this. And I think she'd be quite proud.
(Govan) Oh, no, she'll definitely be very proud. I wish I could name a train after my mom.

(Govan) Through sheer will and determination, this team has turned back the clock 128 years. And it doesn't look like Patricia will run out of steam any time soon.











Promo 1
VO: In Germiston stood a forgotten locomotive.
UPSOUND – Clive Holliday (01:01:52 – 01:01:56):
Govan: This is incredible.
Clive: “When I bought it, it was completely derelict… just a boiler on wheels.”
VO: Seven years of work, and today she’s back on the rails.

Promo 2
VO: To bring Patricia back, it ONLY required a dedicated team and a small fortune.
UPSOUND – Sean Ackermann (01:08:08 – 01:08:34):
“all the wheels were out of the locomotive.… So it was literally just the chassis standing on jacks and stuff. And then putting it in with a jack, you could see now it's becoming a steam locomotive again.
VO: From a bare frame to a working engine — this old steam train lives again.

Promo 3
VO: This locomotive carries more than history.
Clive: This particular locomotive, I actually have some photographs when it was used during the Anglo-Boer War.
VO: Bringing Patricia back meant years of dedication and a small fortune. Once left to rust, this old steam train now runs in all her glory.

Promo 4
(Govan) Where’s the thing you pull to make it… the whistle. Yeah, is that the whistle.
Can I do it? Ah lovely, watch this, watch this. I’ve always wanted to do this.
Oh no, I did it! Its not a great attempt but I did it!
